parts.note: read as a golf putting drill where the ball is holed from every point of a clock face, and also as working through all twelve marked hours

explanation.surface: Someone spends half a day stowing things away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' is the golf stroke, not storing: the drill sets balls at twelve positions round the hole like the hours on a dial, and the phrase also means non-stop work.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means continuously, all day and night, and also names a golf putting practice game played at clock-face positions.

parts.note: read as the fencer's return thrust made straight after deflecting the opponent's blade, while the surface suggests music by the composer Hubert Parry

explanation.surface: A piece of musical counterpoint written in the style of the composer Parry.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised 'Parry' suggests Sir Hubert Parry, the English composer, and 'Counter-point' suggests music; in fencing a parry is followed by a counter-thrust.
explanation.definitionFit: In fencing the quick return attack after deflecting a thrust is this, so it is a counter made after a parry; figuratively a sharp retort.

clue.text: Lord, what a stormy going-away your daughter had

definitions.text: Lord, what a stormy going-away your daughter had

parts.words: Lord, what a stormy going-away your daughter had
parts.note: points to Thomas Campbell's ballad about a chieftain's daughter who elopes across a stormy loch and drowns

explanation.surface: A father is told his daughter's wedding send-off was wild weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lord' looks like an exclamation but is a title: Campbell's poem 'Lord Ullin's Daughter' tells of her flight across a storm-tossed loch with her lover.
explanation.definitionFit: The lord in Thomas Campbell's ballad is named this, and his daughter's elopement ends in a storm on the water.

indicators.note: to worry something about is to toss and shake it around, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A man named Harry frets over the welfare of an old horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worry about' is the anagram signal: HARRY DOES rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Dobbin is a traditional name for a plodding workhorse, such as one pulling a brewer's cart.

clue.text: Is he to be waiting, in drag?

parts.note: taken as the masculine pronoun
taken as the verb, as in 'to be'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man is going to wait tables dressed as a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The goddess Hebe was cupbearer to the Olympian gods; 'he to be' her would be a man waiting in women's clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebe served nectar to the Greek gods, a female waiter, so a man in that role would be in drag.

definitions.note: a verb used for the noun one who steers a boat

parts.note: Cox's Orange Pippin is a well-known English apple variety, shortened to Cox
a swain is an old word for a country labourer or rustic

explanation.surface: A list: an apple, a peasant and some young bulls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steers' looks like cattle; it defines the person who steers, a loose verb-for-noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The person at a boat's helm, especially a rowing boat, directs its course.

definitions.note: Val's brother, the run-together form meaning the brother of Valentine

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
issue means offspring, here a son

explanation.surface: A product called Valbro is made of gold.
explanation.walkthrough: In the medieval romance 'Valentine and Orson' the two are twin brothers, so 'Valbro' means Valentine's brother. The page prints it as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old romance Valentine's twin, raised by a bear, bears this name, so he is the brother of Val.

parts.note: read as careful, gentle treatment, and as gloves made from young goats' skin

explanation.surface: Advice on dealing gently with youngsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'children' is the misdirection: kids are young goats, whose soft leather makes the gloves that stand for delicate treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Treating someone with soft leather mittens made of goatskin is an idiom for very gentle, careful handling.

parts.note: read as the chin whiskers of old jesters, which wagged as they talked

explanation.surface: Jokers have always been jokey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waggish' looks like 'jokey' but means 'given to wagging': the facial hair of talkers traditionally wags, as in the phrase 'while beards wag all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial hair on the chin moves up and down as a man talks, so traditionally it is said to wag.

parts.note: read as the post office box that takes in letters, the communications of 15 across, not a bankruptcy officer

explanation.surface: A court-appointed official who handles insolvencies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Official Receiver' is a real legal title in a bankruptcy; here it is the red British street post box, which receives letters officially.
explanation.definitionFit: A red cylindrical British post box is the Royal Mail's receptacle for posted letters.

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south or southern
an edge is a border or margin

explanation.surface: The southern shore of a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the plant: it grows along lake margins, as in Keats's 'The sedge has withered from the lake'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grassy marsh plant typically lines the margins of lakes and ponds.

clue.text: No cash in change, for the squire backing Dapple

indicators.note: letters in change are being altered, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A squire has no money for his donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in change' signals the anagram of NO CASH. Dapple is the donkey ridden by Don Quixote's squire, who sits on its back.
explanation.definitionFit: Sancho Panza is Don Quixote's squire, who rides the donkey Dapple, so he is the squire on its back.

clue.text: Ask this crook "How do you do ? "

definitions.text: Ask this crook "How do you do ? "

parts.words: Ask this crook "How do you do ? "
parts.note: read as asking a con man how he cheats people, 'do' meaning to cheat

explanation.surface: Greet a criminal politely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How do you do?' is a greeting, but 'do' also means cheat: this crook would explain how he does you.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraudster cheats people out of money, and to cheat someone is to 'do' them.

clue.text: Angel, virago ? A bit of each, Don's girl

indicators.note: a bit of each word is taken, so the answer is spread across the end of one and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Is she an angel or a virago? Some of each, says Don about his girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Giovanni is Mozart's opera; Donna Elvira is one of his abandoned lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Mozart's opera Donna Elvira is a woman seduced and deserted by Don Giovanni.

parts.note: vol is the abbreviation for volume, a book
au vent is French for 'in the wind', a breezy phrase used in English

explanation.surface: A light-hearted book written in English and French.
explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase 'au vent' (in the wind) gives the breeziness; the pastry case is so light it might blow away.
explanation.definitionFit: A small round case of light, flaky pastry, filled with a savoury sauce, is made from puff pastry.

clue.text: Communications for about four young ladies

indicators.note: about here means around, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: misses are young unmarried women
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Messages intended for about four girls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'roughly', as in 'about four', but here it means 'around', the container signal; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal letter is a written message, a kind of communication.

clue.text: Child of the submerged classes : hard case

definitions.text: Child of the submerged classes : hard case

parts.words: Child of the submerged classes : hard case
parts.note: read as a street child from the poorest classes, and as an undersea creature with a hard spiny shell

explanation.surface: A tough slum kid from the underclass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Submerged classes' means the very poor, and 'hard case' a tough person; literally a spiny animal living under the sea in a hard shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiny marine echinoderm with a hard shell; an urchin is also a ragged poor child.

clue.text: One got in a coach in olden times

indicators.note: one piece got into the other, so it sits inside it

parts.note: a stage is a stagecoach

explanation.surface: Someone boarded a stagecoach long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a coach' is the stagecoach of the old coaching days, shortened as it often was; 'got in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The prehistoric era when tools were made of flint is the archetype of very ancient days.

clue.text: Jeeves tucks a pound away gratefully for holiday capital

indicators.note: the manservant tucks the money into himself, so it goes inside

parts.note: Jeeves is P G Wodehouse's famous valet, a gentleman's manservant
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra
ta is British slang for thank you

explanation.surface: A butler pockets a pound tip with thanks before a trip abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucks ... away' puts L in VALET; TA is informal British for 'thanks'. Valletta is the capital of Malta, a holiday island.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Malta is a popular Mediterranean holiday destination.

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
C is the abbreviation for century, a hundred
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A legendary champion from the 500s who lived on a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sixth-century' reads as a date but splits into VI and C.
explanation.definitionFit: A winner or conqueror is a hero, from Latin for one who conquers.

clue.text: Wine, if sound, would scandalize Falstaff

indicators.note: if spoken out loud, the sound matches another phrase

parts.note: Falstaff, Shakespeare's fat knight, loved sack (sherry), so to bar sack would appal him

explanation.surface: A wine whose name, spoken, would shock Shakespeare's Falstaff.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, the name sounds like 'bar sack', banning the sherry Falstaff drinks constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet white wine from the Bordeaux region near Sauternes.

definitions.meaning: marked with an X on a ballot paper to support a candidate

explanation.surface: Someone was blocked while trying to support a party.
explanation.walkthrough: A voter supports a candidate by marking an X on the ballot.
explanation.definitionFit: Thwarted means blocked; and a voter marks a cross beside a candidate's name to support them.

clue.text: Putting heads together, or knocking them

explanation.surface: Working together, or knocking heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubbing together' means pooling; with a club it means hitting people.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooling resources is clubbing together, and hitting someone with a heavy stick is also called this.

parts.note: George Orwell's real surname was shared by a Scottish poet, Robert, author of 'The Grave'

explanation.surface: Orwell was not a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: George Orwell was born Eric Arthur Blair; Robert Blair was an 18th-century Scottish poet, so the poet is that name but not Orwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Blair, Scottish graveyard poet, shared his surname with Orwell's real name.

clue.text: Turn the slave business to art form

indicators.note: turning a word round reads its letters backwards

parts.note: a serf was a bonded labourer, a slave
Co is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: Change the slave trade into an artistic one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' reverses SERF to give FRES, then CO.
explanation.definitionFit: Painting on wet plaster is a mural technique, a kind of art.

clue.text: Gathering of dressmakers to hush-up one with rights

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
I is one in Roman numerals
R is right, so RR is two rights

explanation.surface: Sewing staff must silence one who claims rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gathering' is a dressmaking term, gathered fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathering cloth in parallel rows of stitches is a dressmaking technique.

indicators.note: the word sits in the name, cut short at both ends, so a run of its inner letters is taken

explanation.surface: Wealth is the firepower of Mammon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short' tells you to take a run from inside the name, trimming it at both ends; the result is itself a clipped military word.
explanation.definitionFit: A clipped word for ammunition, the bullets and shells that weapons fire.

definitions.meaning: a musical drama written for the stage

explanation.surface: Something that works on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is the Latin plural of opus, works, and also a single staged musical drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin plural of opus means compositions, and a single sung drama for the theatre has the same name.

clue.text: Provide professors with weapons for sessions ? Easy!

parts.note: to arm is to provide with weapons
chairs are professorships, so professors

explanation.surface: Equip academics with weapons for meetings? Simple!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Easy' is short for easy chairs, comfortable seats for sessions of sitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy chairs are comfortable padded seats with arm rests.

definitions.meaning: a tricorn hat with three corners

explanation.surface: A party election with three candidates.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-party contest and the tricorn hat share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A contest with three candidates and a hat with three points, a tricorn, both have three sides.
